metadata.title: College Savings Bank v. Florida Prepaid Postsecondary Ed. Expense Bd., 527 U.S. 666 (1999) (No. 98-149)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: College Savings Bank v. Florida Prepaid Postsecondary Ed. Expense Bd.

Opinion filed: 1999-06-23

Docket No.: 98-149

Citations:
• 144 L. Ed. 2d 605
• 119 S. Ct. 2219
• 527 U.S. 666
• 1999 U.S. LEXIS 4375

Case holding summaries:
• immunity in suit brought under federal Lanham Act for unfair competition
• allowing Congress to condition the exercise of an Article I power on a state’s agreement to relinquish Eleventh Amendment immunity
• describing these determinations as "stringent," in part because of the Eleventh Amendment’s important federal purpose
• "State does not consent to suit in federal court merely by consenting to suit in the courts of its own creation" or "merely by stating its intention to `sue and be sued.'"
• "The hallmark of a protected property interest is the right to exclude others."
• explaining “[t]he assets of a business (including its good will
• holding that while states may not constructively waive immunity to Lanham Act claims based on term in Trademark Remedy Clarification Act, waiver may be a proper condition on authority granted by Congress that the state would not otherwise have
• "The hallmark of a protected property interest is the right to exclude others."
• "The hallmark of a protected property interest is the right to exclude others."
• noting the circumstances under which Congress may condition the exercise of an Article I power on a state's agreement to relinquish Eleventh Amendment immunity
• holding that Congress did not abrogate states' Eleventh Amendment immunity from suit under Trademark Remedy Clarification Act because Act identified no property right protected by Fourteenth Amendment, whose § 5 enforcement powers were only possible basis for purported abrogation
• noting that Gardner "stands for the unremarkable proposition that a State waives its sovereign immunity by voluntarily invoking the jurisdiction of the federal courts"
• finding no federal jurisdiction for alleged violations of the Lanham Act by state agency
• “Congress may, in the exercise of its spending power, condition its grant of funds to the States upon their taking certain actions that Congress could not require them to take, and . . . acceptance of the funds entails an agreement to the actions”
• "[T]rademarks ... are the `property' of the owner because he can exclude others from using them."
• noting the “clos[e] analogy” between federal and state sovereign immunity
• overruling the constructive waiver doctrine of Parden v. Terminal Railway, 377 U.S. 184, 84 S.Ct. 1207, 12 L.Ed.2d 233 (1964
• noting that Court has recognized individual suits against unconsenting states only when authorized by Congress's valid exercise of its Fourteenth Amendment enforcement power
• noting "our frequent admonition that the Due Process Clause is not merely a 'font of tort law,'" and quoting Paul
• a state does not "constructively waive" Eleventh Amendment immunity by obtaining federally created rights, even when it does so solely as a "market participant"
• effectively foreclosing petitioner's remedy based on finding that Trademark Remedy Clarification Act did not abrogate Florida's sovereign immunity
• "[T]he term `enforce' [in § 5] is to be taken seriously — ... the object of valid § 5 legislation must be the carefully delimited remediation or prevention of constitutional violations."
• finding an individual may sue a state if the state consents to suit or Congress validly abrogates sovereign immunity
• A state's decision to waive its immunity must be "altogether voluntary," and, thus, the "test for determining whether a State has waived its immunity from federal court jurisdiction is a stringent one."
• immunity in suit brought under federal Lanham Act for unfair competition
• describing the "whole point" of the Supreme Court's decision in Hans v. Louisiana, 134 U.S. 1, 10 S.Ct. 504, 33 L.Ed. 842 (1890)
• stating that "constructive waiver is little more than abrogation under another name"
• “The classic description of an effective waiver of a constitutional right is the ‘intentional relinquishment or abandonment of a known right or privilege.’ ”
• recognizing these "two circumstances in which an individual may sue a State"
• stating that "[t]he hallmark of a protected property interest is the right to exclude others" and that this right is "one of the most essential sticks in the bundle of rights that are commonly characterized as property" (internal quotation marks omitted)
• "Congress has no obligation to use its Spending Clause power to disburse funds to the States"
• “[A] state does not . . . consent to suit in federal court merely by stating its intention to ‘sue and be sued.’ ”
• "Recognizing a congressional power to exact constructive waivers of sovereign immunity through the exercise of Article I powers would also, as a practical matter, permit Congress to circumvent the antiabrogation holding of Seminole Tribe."
• "Whatever may remain of our decision in Parden is expressly overruled."
• reiterating "the unremarkable proposition that a State waives its sovereign immunity by voluntarily invoking the jurisdiction of the federal courts"
• describing a statute that concerned "every common carrier" as utilizing "all-embracing language" (emphasis added)
• stating that Gardner, “which held that a bankruptcy court can entertain a trustee’s objections to a claim filed by a State, stands for the unremarkable proposition that a State waives its sovereign immunity by voluntarily invoking the jurisdiction of the federal courts.”
• “[A] State’s sovereign immunity is ‘a personal privilege which it may waive at pleasure.’” (quoting Clark v. Barnard, 108 U.S. 436, 447 (1883))
• federal rejection of constructive waiver
• "Generally, we will find waiver either if the State voluntarily invokes our jurisdiction, or else if the State makes a clear declaration that it intends to submit itself to our jurisdiction."
• courts indulge every reasonable presumption against waiver of fundamental constitutional rights, here, trial by jury
• noting that a state waives its immunity “if the State voluntarily invokes [federal court] jurisdiction, or else if the State makes a clear declaration that it intends to submit itself to [federal court] jurisdiction”
• holding that "a State does not consent to suit in federal court merely by consenting to suit in the courts of its own creation"
• overturning the constructive or implied waiver principle set out in Parden v. Terminal Ry. of Ala. Docks Dep't, 377 U.S. 184 (1964)
• “[A] state does not . . . consent to suit in federal court merely by stating its intention to ‘sue and be sued.’ ”
• "[ Gardner ] held that a bankruptcy court can entertain a trustee's objections to a claim filed by a State, stands for the unremarkable proposition that a State waives its sovereign immunity by voluntarily invoking the jurisdiction of the federal courts."
• by attaching conditions to federal funds, Congress may induce the States to “tak[e] certain actions that Congress could not require them to take”
• “Congress may, in the exercise of its spending power, condition its grant of funds to the States upon their taking certain actions that Congress could not require them to take”
• courts indulge every reasonable presumption against waiver of fundamental constitutional rights, here, trial by jury
• holding that sovereign immunity of State of Florida was neither abrogated by Trademark Remedy Clarification Act, nor voluntarily waived by Florida's activities in interstate commerce
